<reason>Side A won every major clash by anchoring its case in the motion's premise—that these schools are already cutting direct revenue checks—and proving that every problem Side B attributed to collective bargaining is worse under an ad hoc system. Side A cleanly dismantled Side B's scholarship tax scare using the analogy of unionized private-university graduate assistants, neutralized the Olympic sports objection through union voting demographics and sport-specific bargaining units, and turned Side B's complaints about workers' compensation and "managing roster depth" into an indictment of unilateral administrative control. When Side A's first pressure question forced Side B to admit that lawsuit settlements cannot stop future recruits from bringing antitrust suits, Side B had to retreat to wishing for a congressional antitrust exemption—a pivot Side A convincingly exposed in closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's takedown in [A2.4], [A3.2], and [A4.6] of Side B's claim that unions harm coaches' ability to "manage roster depth" and trigger workers' compensation claims—translating "managing roster depth" into cutting injured or underperforming players without recourse, and forcing Side B onto the defensive over why an athlete injured generating millions in TV revenue should be denied workers' compensation and neutral arbitration.</best_rebuttal>
